interviews.title: "We Built a ₹100 Crore Business and Couldn't Raise a Rupee to Save It": The Niro Story
interviews.excerpt: Niro raised $20 million, disbursed $200 million in loans, built $100 million in AUM, and partnered with 30 platforms—then watched a regulatory perfect storm make the business uninvestable.
interviews.body:
Interviewer: Aditya, Niro was a first-mover in embedded consumer lending. When you started in 2021, what was the opportunity you saw?

Aditya Kumar: The idea was simple but powerful. Consumer internet platforms in India had millions of users—people buying on Snapdeal, searching for homes on Housing.com, selling on Quikr. These platforms had distribution and data. Financial institutions had capital but lacked proprietary distribution and differentiated data for underwriting, which fundamentally made their distribution low quality and expensive, and the underwriting commoditised . We positioned Niro in the middle. We would use the platforms' data to underwrite loans and partner with lenders like L&T Finance and Muthoot Finance to provide instant personal loans ranging from ₹50,000 to ₹7 lakh . It worked. We built $100 million in assets under management within two years. At our peak, we processed over 170 million user flows .

Interviewer: That sounds like remarkable traction. What went wrong?

Aditya Kumar: As a first-mover that saw scale quickly, I did not see this coming . The perfect storm hit us from three directions simultaneously. First, regulatory tightening on unsecured personal lending. The RBI became increasingly concerned about the rapid growth of unsecured credit and imposed stricter norms. Second, credit deterioration. The underwriting models that worked in good times started showing cracks as the economic environment shifted. Third, capital availability evaporated. Venture capital funding in digital lending dropped nearly 50% over just eight months . Each of those challenges alone would have been manageable. Together, they were fatal.

Interviewer: You raised $20 million from investors like Elevar Equity, GMO Venture Partners, and Rebright Partners. Wasn't that enough to weather the storm?

Aditya Kumar: Twenty million dollars sounds like a lot until you realise that lending is a capital-intensive business. We needed to raise follow-on funding to sustain operations and grow the loan book. But the market had turned. Unsecured lending platforms were suddenly radioactive for investors. Despite scouring the globe for capital and the country for suitors, I was unable to bring this one home . We approached everyone. Every conversation ended the same way: the regulatory outlook was too uncertain, the credit cycle was too risky. We had done the impossible—hired incredible teams, raised high-quality capital, convinced large consumer internet platforms and leading lenders to work with us—but none of that mattered when the funding window slammed shut .

Interviewer: Did you try to pivot the business model?

Aditya Kumar: We pivoted multiple times. We explored secured lending products. We looked at partnerships that would require less balance sheet exposure. We tried to reposition ourselves as a pure technology infrastructure play rather than a lending platform. But each pivot required time and capital—the two things we didn't have. The regulatory environment was changing faster than we could adapt. And frankly, the fundamental issue remained: financial institutions lack the ability to innovate and build products contextually for consumer internet platforms, and platforms don't speak the language that lenders with ultra-low risk appetites and increased regulatory scrutiny do . That gap is real, but bridging it requires patient capital that simply wasn't available.

Interviewer: What was the moment you knew it was over?

Aditya Kumar: There wasn't one dramatic moment. It was a gradual realisation that the path forward had closed. We had built something real—$200 million in loan disbursements, 30 partnerships, 4.5 years of operation . But we had reached the end of what we could do without fresh capital. When the last acquisition conversation fell through, I knew. I had to tell the team that despite everything we had accomplished, we couldn't continue.

Interviewer: How do you look back on the Niro journey?

Aditya Kumar: I would do it all over again . We were in the right place, at the right time, with the right backing. The thesis was correct: embedded lending is the future of consumer credit in India. The execution was solid. The team was exceptional. We simply ran into a macro environment that no one could have predicted or outrun. I'm grateful to everyone who believed in us—our investors, our platform partners, our lender partners, and most of all, our team. I don't have any immediate plans to start something new. The idea is to decompress a bit . But I remain convinced there's a huge opportunity for AI-enabled infrastructure platforms in embedded financing. With technology and AI, distribution costs are going down drastically. Someone will figure it out.

interviews.title: "Six Failures Before the Seventh Worked": Aman Gupta's Journey to boAt
interviews.excerpt: Aman Gupta failed at six businesses before co-founding boAt at age 36—a brand that would grow to over ₹3,000 crore in annual revenue and make him one of India's most recognizable entrepreneurs.
interviews.body:
Interviewer: Aman, before boAt became a household name, you had six failed ventures. Can you tell us about that journey?

Aman Gupta: I started my entrepreneurial journey at 23. Before boAt, I started and closed six companies. These included a marketing firm called E-Rampage, a children's products brand called CutiePie Lane, an e-commerce platform for musical instruments named Gear Habitat, a social media venture 123.com, and subscription box services like Globtrottersbox.com. Many of these were running simultaneously at one point . The mistake I made repeatedly was that I would just start a company without thinking through the fundamentals. There's a difference between confidence and over-confidence. I would open a big office, hire a huge team, but all my energy was spent managing that instead of focusing on the product we were trying to sell .

Interviewer: That sounds incredibly difficult. How did you sustain yourself financially during those years?

Aman Gupta: It was brutal. My wife Priya was the one who kept our family afloat. She was working, she was earning. I was the one who was failing. She was the one who was running the house . It's not easy to go home at 35 and tell your wife that another idea didn't work. To save money and manage my exhaustion, I would head to the very first stop of a Delhi bus route just to guarantee a seat. I needed that seat not just for the commute, but to catch a few hours of sleep during my 18-hour workdays . My wife eventually gave me an ultimatum—figure out your passion in two years or move on .

Interviewer: What changed when you started boAt in 2016?

Aman Gupta: boAt was my seventh attempt. I was 36. I had learned something crucial from all those failures: focus on the product first, everything else will fall into place. My current office looks and feels like a college canteen—I learned frugality . The idea for boAt came from a simple observation. Sameer Mehta and I noticed that the charging cables available online broke easily. We asked ourselves: why is no one making sturdy, fashionable cables for Indian consumers? We started with an 'indestructible' Apple charging cable, priced at ₹1,500, significantly lower than Apple's original . We pooled ₹30 lakh from our own pockets and started from a small garage-like room in Delhi's Okhla area .

Interviewer: What made boAt different from your previous ventures?

Aman Gupta: Timing, execution, and understanding the Indian consumer. When we started, there were no Indian brands in the audio space. There was a colonial hangover—Indians used to hate Indian brands. They were not respected . We saw that young India wanted quality audio and fashionable products, but they didn't want to pay Apple prices. We positioned boAt in the ₹500 to ₹5,000 price range. Affordable premium. That was the gap . We focused on style and strength—bright colors, strong bass, fun taglines. We targeted young users who love music and photos.

Interviewer: There was also a personal tragedy that shaped your perspective, wasn't there?

Aman Gupta: I lost my brother in a tragic accident on his own birthday. When you see life and death like that, you realize that business is just a game. I stopped being scared of failing because I had already seen the worst . After that, the usual pressures of running a business just didn't seem as heavy anymore. I learned to enjoy every day, even when I had no money for nearly six years building boAt . Staying happy is my utmost priority now.

Interviewer: boAt grew rapidly. What were some of the challenges along the way?

Aman Gupta: Revenue isn't profit. FY23 we did ₹3,377 crore in revenue but still had a ₹98 crore loss . The D2C audio market is ruthless. Heavy marketing spend, discount wars, brutal competition, squeezed margins. We had to learn and adapt. We cut weak product lines, increased prices with our 'Nirvana' series for premium customers, and expanded exports . You have to change or fade. That's the reality.

Interviewer: You recently stepped down from your operational role as CMO. Why?

Aman Gupta: It was a long-term plan to professionalise the organization. About three years ago, we brought in an external CEO. We believe it is high time that professionally run management takes over . Another reason is that I am a strong founder. When a strong founder still works in the system, employees feel there are many bosses in the company. I want Gaurav to run the company as if there is only one boss—and that's him . I stepped down before the IPO because I didn't think it would be fair to retail investors if they invested believing I was running the company and then suddenly someone else took over .

Interviewer: What advice do you have for entrepreneurs who are struggling through failure right now?

Aman Gupta: In life, we all face downs. I have been down too, more times than one can imagine. But when you hit rock bottom, there is only one way out—up. Keep hustling. The day you stop trying is the day you fail . The lessons you learn from failures, you cannot learn from anywhere else. What marketing you learn in business school and what you actually have to use in real life are very different. I learned more from my six failures than I ever learned in a classroom . Don't take life too seriously. Work hard, but remember that the music can stop at any time .

interviews.title: "We Were Profitable but Too Small to Matter": The Satvacart Story
interviews.causeOfFailure: Inability to Scale Against Quick Commerce Giants
interviews.excerpt: Satvacart survived twelve years by doing the one thing its competitors refused to do—focus on profitability. That same discipline made it too small to raise capital or find a buyer.
interviews.body:
Interviewer: Rahul, Satvacart was one of India's earliest online grocery startups. When you started in 2014, what was the vision?

Rahul H. Saxena: We started with milk subscriptions in Gurugram. It was a simple idea—deliver fresh milk to people's doorsteps before they wake up. At the time, online grocery was barely a concept in India. BigBasket was still finding its feet. Grofers was just getting started. We saw an opportunity to build something that actually worked for the Indian consumer, not just for investors. We transitioned to an inventory-led grocery delivery model through micro-clusters, with independent warehouses serving customers within a five-kilometre radius. It was hyperlocal before hyperlocal was a buzzword .

Interviewer: You raised seed funding in 2015. Did you feel pressure to scale aggressively like your competitors?

Rahul H. Saxena: We did raise seed funding from Palaash Ventures and angel investors. The plan was to expand operations, acquire customers, and strengthen our technology team. But we made a deliberate choice to take a more measured approach. We focused on profitability while competitors burned cash on customer acquisition. By 2019, we became one of the early online grocery companies to demonstrate profitability in the category . I was proud of that. But I didn't realize then that profitability without scale would become our Achilles' heel.

Interviewer: What changed in the market that made things difficult?

Rahul H. Saxena: Quick commerce happened. Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart—they completely transformed how Indians bought groceries online. Delivery in ten minutes. Dark stores everywhere. Massive funding. The game shifted from scheduled deliveries and hyperlocal grocery to speed and density. We were competing in a market that no longer valued what we offered. The past few years were particularly challenging. Capital came in, but largely in small tranches rather than at the scale required to rebuild and grow the business .

Interviewer: Did you try to raise more funding or find a buyer?

Rahul H. Saxena: We explored every realistic option. We were in discussions with two larger investors for significant funding. Neither deal materialized. We also had acquisition talks with multiple companies, but those did not go through either . The feedback was consistent: we hadn't built enough scale to make the conversations attractive. Our focus on profitability meant we remained relatively small at a time when scale became increasingly important to raising capital or finding a buyer . The irony is that the very discipline that kept us alive for twelve years made us unattractive to the people who could have saved us.

Interviewer: What was the moment you knew it was over?

Rahul H. Saxena: There came a point where continuing operations was coming at the cost of people who had stood by the company . I couldn't keep asking my team to sacrifice when I no longer believed we could win. The past few months had become increasingly difficult. August 28, 2026, was our last day of operations. The team was disbanded. I made the decision to stop and move on .

Interviewer: How do you look back on twelve years of building Satvacart?

Rahul H. Saxena: I have no regrets. Building Satvacart involved everything—technology, operations, fundraising, marketing, supply chain, customer experience. I gave it the very best effort I was capable of . We proved that an online grocery business could be profitable in India. We proved that you could build something sustainable without burning investor money recklessly. The market eventually decided that profitability alone wasn't enough. But I'd rather have built something real that lasted twelve years than something flashy that collapsed in two.

Interviewer: What are you doing next?

Rahul H. Saxena: I'm transitioning into a role at the intersection of business, tech, AI, and marketing at a Series B+ startup. I'm also considering launching a new venture eventually, though I haven't decided what that looks like yet . As this chapter closes, I look forward to the next one .

interviews.title: "We Expanded Faster Than the System Could Digest": The Ayurveda Co's Cautionary Tale
interviews.excerpt: The Ayurveda Co scaled to over ₹150 crore in GMV, raised ₹125 crore from investors, and built a team of more than 1,000 people—then discovered that a small baby with too many mothers cannot survive.
interviews.body:
Interviewer: Shreedha and Param, The Ayurveda Co was once one of India's most visible D2C beauty brands. When did you first realize the company was in trouble?

Shreedha Singh Bhargava: I have post-mortemed every significant and small decision gazillion times over, trying to figure out which one could have been the inflection point for a different outcome . The honest answer is that there was no single moment. It was a slow unraveling. We expanded too fast, too wide, and brought on way too many senior folks too early on, before the system could digest. A small baby had too many mothers .

Param Bhargava: I take full responsibility for what did not work. We scaled to more than ₹150 crore in annual GMV. We had over 1,000 people across on-roll and off-roll roles. At our peak, we had 20 owned stores, 800 beauty-adviser counters, more than 10,000 touch points, and 110 operational distributors . On paper, it looked like we had built something substantial. But the infrastructure—the internal systems, the processes, the organizational clarity—could not keep pace with the growth.

Interviewer: You raised ₹125 crore from venture capital and angel investors. Was funding not enough to sustain the expansion?

Param Bhargava: Funding was never the problem. The problem was how we deployed it. We built too much, too soon. We hired senior leadership before we had the operational maturity to support them. We entered channels and categories before we had proven unit economics. When funding tightened across the ecosystem in 2024 and 2025, the cracks that were already there became canyons . The mistake wasn't raising money. It was assuming that money could solve structural problems.

Interviewer: The broader Indian startup ecosystem saw a wave of shutdowns in 2025—Dunzo, BluSmart, Hike, Good Glamm Group. Did you see yourselves heading toward the same fate?

Shreedha Singh Bhargava: We were aware of what was happening around us. But every founder believes they are different. We told ourselves that our category—Ayurveda and wellness—had tailwinds. We told ourselves that our customer love was real. And it was. But customer love does not pay for an overextended cost structure. The failures around us were not just about funding winters. They were about discipline. And we were not disciplined enough.

Interviewer: What specifically went wrong with the expansion strategy?

Param Bhargava: We confused activity with progress. Opening stores, signing distributors, launching new SKUs, hiring senior people—these all felt like growth. But they were just multiplication of complexity. The Ayurveda Co and Khadi Essentials together generated ₹250 crore in net revenue over seven years and reached 20 lakh consumers . Those are real achievements. But the cost of acquiring and serving those consumers kept rising faster than the revenue they generated. We were running a business where contribution margins were thin or negative, and scaling that only made the losses bigger.

Interviewer: Did you consider pulling back and restructuring earlier?

Shreedha Singh Bhargava: We tried. Param and I mortgaged our parental property. We did not withdraw salaries for more than a year. We fought very, very hard to keep the boat afloat . But by the time we realized the magnitude of the problem, we were already too deep. The decision to shut down operations in July 2025 was the hardest one we have ever made. I'd rather say this out loud than let it quietly disappear .

Interviewer: What would you say to other Indian D2C founders who are scaling aggressively right now?

Param Bhargava: Build boringly strong businesses. That is the lesson . Growth without repeatability, revenue without unit economics, teams without accountability—these are the cracks that widen into chasms. The Indian market is large, but it is also unforgiving. You can have millions of users and still fail if those users do not translate into sustainable revenue. I would tell every founder to ask themselves: if funding disappeared tomorrow, could my business survive on its own cash flows? If the answer is no, you do not have a business. You have a bet.

Shreedha Singh Bhargava: And I would add this: do not let ambition outrun your capacity to execute. We had a beautiful brand. We had loyal customers. We had a mission that mattered. But a mission without operational rigor is just a story. We learned that the hard way. I am now contemplating what my next purpose looks like as this chapter closes . Whatever it is, I will carry these lessons with me.

interviews.title: We Built for a Market That Didn't Exist Yet
interviews.excerpt: Sanjay Swamy tried to build mobile payments in India a decade before UPI made it a reality — and learned that being right too early is indistinguishable from being wrong.
interviews.body:
Interviewer: Sanjay, mChek was one of India's earliest attempts at mobile payments. When did the idea first come to you?

Sanjay Swamy: It started with an auto rickshaw driver. I had just returned from Silicon Valley to India in the early 2000s. I asked this driver what the time was, and he pulled out a cell phone. That was the aha moment for me — he has a terminal in his hands. At the time, mobile phones were spreading rapidly across India, even among lower-income consumers. But banking penetration was extremely limited. Only a fraction of the country had formal bank accounts. I saw an opportunity to bridge those two worlds. The value proposition looked compelling for everyone .

Interviewer: What was the core premise of mChek?

Sanjay Swamy: We wanted to turn mobile phones into wallets. Consumers would no longer need to stand in long queues to pay electricity bills or recharge prepaid mobile plans. Telcos would reduce customer churn. Banks would gain active digital users. Payments would become frictionless. What we were attempting to do — saying people will be using their mobile phones to make payments — that was clearly going to happen. It was a matter of when and not a matter of if .

Interviewer: But the timing proved to be the problem, didn't it?

Sanjay Swamy: India in 2006 was not merely pre-UPI. It was pre-smartphone, pre-app store, and pre-Aadhaar. There were 14 telecom operators in the country. Today we have three. People switched SIM cards constantly because telecom companies were aggressively competing for market share. Mobile number portability did not exist. Internet penetration was weak. SMS packs were a major consumer product. Nokia had probably 75 to 80% market share at the time. People were still paying several rupees per minute for calling .

Interviewer: So the infrastructure simply wasn't there.

Sanjay Swamy: The perception in the market at the time was that if you needed to do anything on the mobile phone, you had to partner with the telco. That dependency became one of the defining challenges of mChek. Fundamentally, the world over, telcos and banks don't trust each other. Everybody told me they will not work with each other. Our model required telecom operators, banks, Visa, and regulators to cooperate simultaneously. Each stakeholder had different priorities. The only thing that mattered to telecom operators was the land grab and establishing themselves. Banks were deeply conservative. There was no regulation. The mobile was not accepted or seen as anything the regulator thought needed to be regulated .

Interviewer: You actually worked with the RBI on early mobile banking guidelines, didn't you?

Sanjay Swamy: We managed to get the first version of the mobile banking guidelines out. I found myself spending time with the RBI helping shape India's earliest mobile banking regulations. But shaping regulation and building a business are two very different things. The ecosystem complexity was overwhelming. We were trying to coordinate players who had no incentive to coordinate .

Interviewer: Looking back, was there a specific moment when you realized mChek wouldn't survive?

Sanjay Swamy: I think we always knew we were ahead of the curve. The question was whether we could survive long enough for the curve to catch up. We couldn't. The funding environment for something that required such deep ecosystem coordination was brutal. Investors could see the vision, but they couldn't see the path. And frankly, neither could we — not with the clarity that a business requires.

Interviewer: What would you say to founders today who believe they're building something the market isn't ready for?

Sanjay Swamy: There's a fine line between being a visionary and being a fool. The difference is usually timing. If you're too early, you burn capital educating a market that isn't ready to buy. The market doesn't reward being right. It rewards being right at the right time. We were right about mobile payments. We were wrong about 2006.

Interviewer: Do you regret building mChek?

Sanjay Swamy: Not for a moment. The lessons were invaluable. I learned more from failing at mChek than I would have from succeeding at something easier. The entire ecosystem that exists today — UPI, QR codes, digital wallets — those are the children of the ideas we were experimenting with. We didn't get to see the harvest, but we helped plant the seeds.

interviews.title: How Flexiple Reached $1M ARR in 4 Years and $2M in 4 Months
interviews.excerpt: Karthik co-founded Flexiple, an offshore team and GCC building company that builds and runs India teams end to end. After 4 years, they've fully bootstrapped it to $2M in annual revenue and have been growing at ~25%+ MoM in the past 5 months.
interviews.body:
Hi Karthik! Who are you and what are you currently working on?
I am Karthik, Co-founder and CEO of Flexiple, a network of pre-vetted freelance developers & designers to help top startups & companies find quality tech talent. At Flexiple, my responsibilities include marketing and tech while my co-founders handle the more difficult job of everything freelancer & client operations-related.

Before Flexiple, I worked in JPMorgan as an Investment Banker - quite a different job & role as compared to the world of startups I am in now! However, after spending 3 years there, I realized it wasn’t for me and soon started my journey with Flexiple.

Now, after investing 4 full years into Flexiple, we have fully bootstrapped it to $2million in annual revenue and have been growing at ~25%+ m-o-m in the past 5 months. Simple business model - our freelance talent set their rates and we take a commission from clients on each project.



What's your backstory and how did you come up with the idea?
Immediately, after my time at JPMorgan, I wasn’t entirely sure what I wanted to do next. But, when I got through the top MBA university in India, I felt that it might give me the time to explore my next steps.

But on joining the MBA school, the noise around job placements pushed me towards starting something of my own. So, I used to carry around an idea book noting down different ideas that I felt I would enjoy working on. In the process, I recognized that B2B was the space where I would like to spend my time building a startup.

Of the many ideas, I found Flexiple to be the most interesting because:

Most other freelance marketplaces catered to the “gig economy” - where quality is not the focus, rather the volume is. Whereas, Flexiple plays in the “talent economy” where quality is at the core of everything we do and I felt there was still a huge opportunity there.
Further, I believed that the future would involve more & more people being focused on building individual brands vs. just being a small cog of a larger monolithic company.
Also, tech as a functional vertical was continuing to grow massively in size - all startups have tech as their backbone. Top this with the fact that hiring in tech is just brutally painful.
So, we recognized a real problem - building a high-quality tech talent network that can help startups & companies in hiring. The question was largely about whether we could execute and make things happen.



How did you go from idea to product?
Honestly, our first two products were absolute failures. We spent $5000 to build each one and ended up throwing each into the bin. In the end, we just used a simple GoogleSheet to make our first $100k in revenue. I have written about it in detail in this thread, but let me explain our mistake briefly here.

There are largely two types of tech startups:

“Tech-enabled”: where tech just enables you to scale. For e.g. Uber, Airbnb, etc.
“Core-tech” where tech is part of your core offering. E.g. Dropbox, Postman, etc.
Many startups are just the former but confuse themselves to be the latter. 

The consequences of this confusion are that:

They invest way too much time building tech to solve future challenges of scale, instead of focusing on building their business and infusing tech when manual efforts have become a bottleneck
Further, trying to build tech before experiencing the real bottlenecks means that you are trying to predict them, which hardly ever works.
We made the same mistake. Our customers - freelancers & clients - didn’t care too much about the product we had made. The former wanted quality projects and the latter, great talent. We were just forcing our product on them.

When we realized this, we just moved all our work to a simple Google sheet, with our website functioning largely for marketing purposes. All flows thereafter were manual - using emails, manually sending invoices, and so on. This allowed us to focus on actually delivering value to our customers while not being preoccupied about scaling the business from the word go.

Flexiple Landing Page
Which were your marketing strategies to grow your business?
For the initial year, almost all the business we got was through our network. We leveraged LinkedIn to find the right person in the companies we wanted as clients and just hustled our way to get our first 10-20 clients. I wrote about the entire process in detail in this thread.



However, soon we hit a ceiling. We recognized that our target audience was startups in the US, Europe, etc. - tech startups that wanted quality tech talent and could afford them. Given our network was ZERO outside India, we realized we had to work on growing our inbound pipeline.



We found ProductHunt to be quite useful for us. Most startups only launch their primary product on PH, but we also made many “side projects”, which we launched on PH and marketed Flexiple subtly in them. More about it here.

However, it wasn’t a very reliable and stable channel. That’s when we invested heavily in SEO and that’s been a real journey. It involved:

Build our “Domain authority” by writing many guest posts
Then we identified keywords that had high intent. This would involve our competitor alternatives-type keywords on which we wrote focused blogs such as “Toptal alternative” which gave us many client leads.
But beyond that, we made a ton of marketing pages targeting low-volume keywords but with very high conversion intent. E.g. A page for “Hire Freelance React Developers” => We would then just replace the word “React” with any other technology and duplicate the pages. Of course, we had to have enough unique content on each page to ensure we weren’t penalized by Google for duplicate content.
This SEO strategy laid the foundation for our inbound growth - though it took a lot of mistakes and about a year to pay off in a big way. We have since gotten even better at SEO and have ~100k people visiting our website each month.

Flexiple Visitors
However, one of the pleasant consequences of ensuring our customers are really happy is that a major source of revenue comes from repeat customers and customer referrals - about ~40%.

In the past 4-5 months, both my co-founder and I have become more active on Twitter & LinkedIn which has also become a great channel for new leads.



How are you doing today and what are your goals for the future?
It has been a slow burn for us - it took us almost 4 years to get to $1million in annual revenue. However, in just another four months, we are $2million in annualized revenue -  we have been growing at ~25%+ m-o-m in the past 5 months.

Flexiple Website
Honestly, it isn’t that we have suddenly cracked a hidden code - it is just that our efforts in the past many years are paying dividends now. Of course, we are making fewer mistakes in execution now :).

I feel, we have found what I can define as replicable success - so now our focus has shifted to consolidating this while ensuring we build a great team around us. We have laid the initial foundation of a quality team with ~20 of us in the team.

Being a fully remote team, we don’t have location constraints but still have other hiring bottlenecks and team engagement techniques to solve for. We haven’t gotten great at that yet and that’s one of my goals in the next 6 months.

Furthermore, we are big believers in remote working. Since 2018, we have been building Remote Tools and more recently, Remote Clan. While I am proud of what we have been able to accomplish with these two, we haven’t monetized them yet. I hope to change that in the coming months.

Since starting Flexiple, what have been your main lessons?
Being a first-time entrepreneur, there were many mistakes we made, and a few things I realized include:

Don’t build for scale before you have earned a single dollar - focus on business before being obsessed with tech.
Building in constraints is good - it ensures that you don’t have the luxury to indulge yourself in stupid decisions for long. It aligns you to do the best for your customer as that’s the only REAL way to make money.
Start working on SEO, being active on social media and other communities as early as possible.
There are easier ways to make money than entrepreneurship. Therefore, starting up for money is not the best idea because you will find it tough to sustain your motivation.
Startups test your patience and the ability to do boring & repetitive things over long periods. If you can survive through it, the results are exponential.


What were the biggest obstacles you overcame? What were your worst mistakes?
The biggest obstacle we overcame would be the ability to generate quality inbound traffic and as a result, good leads. None of us (the three co-founders) were active on social media or knew much about marketing. I just made my social accounts last year.

Of course, one has to find the relevant channel for them to leverage, but in our case, we realized that just adding value on the mainstream social channels like Twitter and LinkedIn would help us grow our own business too.

Also, learning SEO was critical but we started too late. For a couple of years, we wrote articles that were never optimized and therefore didn’t bring us any traffic. So, in all honesty, they were wasted efforts.

We, of course, learned from our initial mistakes of building tech before actually needing it or understanding what to build. Since then, we have been gradually infusing it as we scale. Even now, ironically, all our tech is set up on NoCode tools as it gets the job done extremely well.

‍

What tools & resources do you recommend?
Don’t build landing pages from scratch. Use builders like Unicorn and Umso.
Use NoCode tools like Bubble, Webflow, Adalo, etc. to validate your idea and make good money before investing heavily in tech
For SEO, don’t use free tools. Ahrefs is worth the money
Other than that, just get your hands dirty by actually doing things and keep googling things you don’t know or can’t understand :)

interviews.title: Failing to Scale an Indian AgriTech Startup with $335k ARR
interviews.excerpt: Tarun co-founded Freshconnect, an online B2B marketplace for fresh agricultural produce like fruits & vegetables. After making mistakes like lack of focus and bad hiring, they couldn't secure a funding round and eventually got acqui-hired by another company.
interviews.body:
Hi Tarun! Who are you and what are you currently working on?
My name is Tarun Gupta and I'm 26 years old. I did my schooling in a small town near Sirsa, Haryana but I'm currently based out of Bangalore, a metropolitan city in Karnataka, India. Nowadays, I'm heading supply chain ops at Evenflow Brands, which buys & builds e-commerce first brands. 

Freshconnect was an online B2B marketplace for fresh agricultural produce like fruits & vegetables. I was co-founder & COO and was responsible for operations, business development & finance verticals majorly. Anyway, you practically need to keep an eye on all areas of an early-stage startup as a founder. 

We had a very simple business model where we used to charge a margin on top of cost price for the products & delivery charge for the logistics services to our customers.

‍

What’s your background and how did you come with FreshConnect’s idea?
I hail from a lower-middle-class family in a small town but I have always been a curious and aspirational person since my childhood. In our society, if you are an above-average student you either go for engineering or medical for your undergraduate studies. I chose engineering as I liked maths and went on to prepare for JEE (Entrance examination for getting into prestigious engineering colleges IITs). After failing once and in my final attempt, I got into IIT Delhi (top 3 engineering college of India). College was a lot of fun, I got to explore my identity after seeing people from diverse backgrounds. Also, I got to learn about entrepreneurship for the first time while doing my first internship for a startup that was operating from the dorm room of my college in 2013.

After that, I tried to start my own company and after trying multiple ideas, when nothing evolved into something tangible and with a lot of pressure from family, I was forced to take up a supply chain consulting job through campus placements. 

Even after joining the job, I used to try to be updated on what was happening in the startup ecosystem and tried to brainstorm ideas on weekends. A few months later, I was exposed to the conditions of the Indian farmers when I saw hunger strikes and farmer rallies happening all over the country. Looking at this, I realized that it was the inefficiency and unfair practices involved in this sector that lead to low farmer incomes. I started researching this field with the idea of connecting farmers directly to markets. After a few months of working part-time on this project, I finally decided to take this up full-time by quitting my job. The initial idea was called FarmConnect and consisted on connecting farmers to markets. I was working on this with a high school student who was passionate about entrepreneurship too. But later on, it didn’t work out and I was left with no job and no co-founder. 

But I kept working on the idea and started talking to people in my network who were working on solving similar problems. One of my seniors from IIT Delhi connected me to Amit Kashyap, who was also my senior at college. After graduating from IIT Delhi in Electrical Engineering, Amit started his career with Honeywell Aerospace as a Senior Engineer in 2015. As he worked on system engineering techniques for Aircraft Maintenance IT Solutions, Amit always wanted to work for society and create an impact. This led him to the conditions of Indian Agricultural Producers and he grew passionate about this cause. On gaining a fair understanding of the inefficiency in this sector, he started working on bringing markets closer to the producers. Around the same time I got in touch with him and after a few discussions and debates in the initial stage, I and Amit decided to go ahead with the idea of FreshConnect.

Prior to FreshConnect, while in college, there was an important moment in my entrepreneurship journey. In my second year, a guy with a diary in his hand knocked on my door. He explained to me that he had a business opportunity that didn't require investing a lot of money or resources. It was a multilevel marketing business, where you earned passive income by growing your network; just like the Amway model. In my desperation to do something, I thought this was a sign and I took the opportunity by spending INR15000 of my college scholarship on that. This guy later convinced me to spend INR25000 more, so as to be able to get success faster. It was all logical for me at that point, so I did invest all my scholarship amount of that semester. Unlike other MLM companies, they were giving products worth the same amount I was investing, but the problem is that no one needed them.

On top of that, I flunked my studies to completely focus on my business and justified it by looking at examples like Bill Gates who dropped out of college to start their business. I performed very poorly that semester, lost my scholarship money and soured a lot of relationships with my friends by selling this opportunity to them. This also hurt my mental health as I went into mild depression (without knowing it). I was ashamed of myself because of this failure and I didn’t tell my parents about this until everything fell apart. 

But this experience taught me a lot of life lessons: 

It's not worth fulfilling your ambitions at the cost of precious relationships. 
That I am good at sales. I did great in selling memberships as the first time selling something. I used to show them the big picture after trying to understand their motivations in life then. 
I should not put all the eggs in one basket especially in the case of startups which are very risky endeavors. 
There should be a fine balance of emotion & rationalism while making these decisions.
How did you go from idea to product?
One month before I left the job (July 2018): 

Amit and I had different ideas for the startup. While I was trying to connect farmers to markets, he was trying to create an online marketplace for businesses & farmers alike. But there were a lot of similarities so we decided to brainstorm the ideas together and come up with a common framework to work these ideas out.

At that time, I came across the book Disciplined Entrepreneurship by Bill Aulet, a professor at MIT Sloan. He had created 24 steps to build a successful startup. We used this framwork to define our target segments and figure out the most pressing problem these segments had.

We decided that we wanted to solve problems for retailers in the procurement of fresh produce. For that, we needed to learn what their problems were  by talking to them.

Besides this, Amit had already hired a fresh graduate who was a software developer to help him build the tech product.

After I left the Job (Aug 2018): 

We drafted a list of questions inspired by the book and started going to retail stores in nearby areas trying to understand their current purchasing process and problems they were encountering.

Also on the side, Amit & the hired developer started working on the tech product as basic wireframes, etc. were already in place from the work that Amit had done before FreshConnect. Amit also convinced 2 experienced software engineers to come on board part-time to build the backend & frontend. Moreover, we brought 1 more team member who was from our college and a junior of Amit in order to handle operations along with me. 

Part of pre-accelerator (Sept 2018):

Until this point we were on our own and being first-time entrepreneurs, trying different things. I started applying to accelerators and similar programs to be part of the ecosystem as well as to get mentorship.

We applied to an equity-free pre-accelerator called Startup Launchpad and got selected. The commitment was a few hours on the weekend and they helped us with doing customer interviews and with our GTM strategy.

With their help, we launched the same month with 1 customer, to whom we delivered the products on our bikes. We hadn't built any tech yet and we were still heavily using WhatsApp for customer communication and GDocs for all our internal planning. 

Tech Product Launch (Mar 2019) 

We did a lot of experiments with Whatsapp & other free tools to understand customer behavior initially before launching our product.

We initially planned to launch the tech product in Dec 2018 but it got delayed by 3-4 months because of the challenges around DevOps or expectation mismatch from our teammates who were working part-time.

Finally, in Mar 2019, we launched a web application where users could log in using their phone number and OTP, see all the categories of products in a structured format and add to cart. However, there was no checkout system. Orders were finished through Whatsapp. We wanted to launch faster and Amit came up with this hack.

We initially used Firebase for beta but we then shifted to AWS (free account for 1 year with limited options) as our server.

There was another challenge that we faced which was related to our target audience: retailers were not tech-savvy and we needed to push them to order through the app. I think this push is needed to change existing user behavior. While well-capitalized players do it through giving deep discounts, we did it manually.

FreshConnect Landing
Burning Money (Oct 2019)

We grew 10-15% month on month and till this point we were completely bootstrapped, unable to raise outside capital but at the same time, we were losing money m/m due to operations cost & defaults in credits by customers.

In October 2019, I did some calculations and realized that we only had one month of runway left with our existing resources. It was a wake-up call for everyone. We immediately took a small loan of Rs. 3Lacs on the company. However, it was still a small amount for the long term; we needed to raise equity capital.

The motivation of the team start going down as we started losing our monthly growth. My co-founder took a break in Nov 2019 and went to his hometown. During that time, I kept trying to keep the boat afloat as much as possible and looking for ways to raise money in desperation.

FreshConnect Delivery


Which were the strategies to grow your business?
We didn’t do any paid marketing in our journey of FreshConnect as we wanted to grow organically. We were not present on any social media platform. We onboarded our customers through offline sales and used WhatsApp for communicating offers.

I think customers were very responsive on WhatsApp as more than 390M users use it in India. Offline sales worked well as it allowed us to understand the problem of the customer and accordingly position our solution, which resulted in better sales.

When did things start to go in the wrong direction?
Check out my reflections on this question here.

At a personal level, inexperience was our disadvantage. I & my co-founder were recent graduates from the same college and I know that a lot of founders start right out of college but that should be balanced by a mentor or advisor who helps you to understand the macro view of things. As first-time entrepreneurs, we made many mistakes in hiring, business model, and GTM strategy, but the biggest mistake was not being nimble. We got stuck with the initial team and business model for long enough for us to not be able to come out of it successfully.



Which were the causes of FreshConnect’s failure?
There was not a single reason for our failure. We made bad hiring decisions initially as well as didn’t fire bad elements at the right time, set up wrong expectations from each other (as co-founders), did not work much on financial planning, took the initial interest of investors for granted which didn’t lead into investment, among other reasons.

We started raising outside capital very late in the journey. We had real-time feedback with customers but not with investors which, in my opinion, is equally important and helps you to have a macro view of the model along with a micro view of problems that you are trying to solve.

A lot of founders think that media or marketing is just to reach customers, but it's super important to reach to investors as well. No investors had heard about us even though we had achieved better metrics than others in the ecosystem. This is another mistake that did cost us our company. 

We also lacked focus initially and spread ourselves too thin as per our limited resources. This led to us achieving inappropriate metrics which made it hard for us to raise external funds which were necessary for our business model. 

I remember that we had a healthy revenue growth rate month on month but didn’t have the financial backup to sustain it for long and we were desperate for capital. We already had initial interest from 2 angel investors and we were relying on this capital to survive. Both deals fell through within a week due to the investor’s reasons. This seemed like the end of it but I was still optimistic and tried to curtail expenses and increase our efforts on fundraising so that we could survive. 

My co-founder had a mental breakdown and we all suggested that he took a break for some time. It was tough for me to manage  this situation but this was the right thing to do. He went home and started getting better. But then I got a call from him after a few weeks telling me he couldn't take it anymore and wanted to quit. I think this was a mental breakpoint for everyone. Slowly, other team members started to quit too.

I tried to get an M&A deal for a month but without any success. Eventually, my co-founder came back and helped me to get an acqui-hire deal with another large company. The rest of our team joined the other company along with the transfer of our whole business. FreshConnect went on as it was and even grew more than 6x in the acquirer company.

‍

Which were your expenses? Did you achieve any revenue? In the end, how much money did you lose?
MRR: INR 2,500,000

ARR: INR 25,000,000

Burn (Expenses-Revenue): INR 100,000-150,000/month

Money invested: Rs. 1,500,000 (Founder’s savings & loan)

Time Spent: 19 months (full time). 6 months (part time)

‍

If you had to start over, what would you do differently?
Find the right co-founder (preferably someone you know) and have as many hard conversations as possible before committing to starting up. Set the right expectations from day one.
Focus on making one thing successful rather than spreading yourself too thin. 
Think hard on your finances as that is the fuel that keeps a startup going. Work on raising capital early if needed. 
Hiring decisions are the most costly one, so take time and effort to make the right initial hires. Set right expectations and sell them the bigger vision.
At the initial stages, I wish we should have spent more time on hiring, fundraising & talking to users rather than increasing our sales and revenue. Also, I should have spent more time working on our finances and less on optimizing ops.

interviews.title: Helping 3,000+ Businesses Talk to Their Customers with a No-Code Chat Marketing Tool
interviews.excerpt: Mitul founded WotNot, an all-in-one chat marketing tool that helps businesses develop a pipeline of qualified leads, increase revenue and retain clients without adding more employees. He founded the company with five friends, and they now are 140 people.
interviews.body:
Hi Mitul! Who are you & what are you currently working on?
I am Mitul Makadia, the Founder & CEO of Maruti Techlabs and WotNot.

Maruti Techlabs is a product development company that assists small and medium-sized businesses and enterprises in their digital transformation endeavors. We do it all, from bringing ideas to life through rapid application development to enhancing processes with RPA and AI to expediting customer service with chatbots.

Our mission is to assist our clients in developing future-proof and intuitive digital products and lead them through the finest procedures and practices for a successful digital transformation and long-term scaling.

We've built products for customers in 16 industries over the last decade, and we've also built and are scaling two of our own.

WotNot is one of them: an all-in-one chat marketing tool that helps businesses develop a pipeline of qualified leads, increase revenue and retain clients without adding to their workforce. We simply help you communicate with your present and potential consumers at scale now.

Our approach towards product development is based on a combination of the lean startup methodology and the Agile Scrum framework. Our love for delivering excellent products is deep-rooted, and it’s what drives us to take each assignment with a fresh perspective and great commitment.



What's your backstory and how did you come up with the idea?
After graduation, I worked for nearly 5 years as a Senior Technical Manager for a product engineering firm. In 2009, I founded Maruti Techlabs with a single assignment for a client in the United States. 

Our story begins with ones. One small assignment, one diligent team, one trusting client, one bold deal. It all started with a simple task for a dependable client. I'm delighted to say that we continue to work for that client. 

Since then, we've been cutting our teeth in digital transformation solutions with trailblazing products that set a new standard for conducting smart business.

‍

How did you go from idea to product?
One of our long-term clients approached us with a problem that almost every business struggles with. Their limited customer support staff was inundated with daily calls, which led to extended wait times and increased business expenses. Poor customer experience led to a below-par brand image and a significant loss to the business.

As a result, we created a chatbot to address this troubling problem. We planned to build an easy-to-use chatbot and live chat platform based on their excellent achievements to reproduce favorable results for other companies across industries.

As a result, WotNot was born. WotNot has been assisting businesses in reducing costs and improving the customer experience since then. 

We take pride in our simplistic chatbot platform, which stands out in the crowd of complicated and technical chatbot services.

WotNot Landing Page
Which were your marketing strategies to grow your business?
We tried and tested a lot of things. But the following stuck and has helped us get to where we are today:

Content development and marketing
SEO & CRO
Customer reviews and referrals
Product Hunt launch
Going Freemium
Integration marketplace
Interviews and listings
WotNot Growth Hacking Strategies
‍

How are you doing today and what are your goals for the future?
We're doing fantastic. Since our first project, we’ve been a go-to technical and product development partner for clients in the automotive, advertising, eCommerce, healthcare, and other industries. In 2009, I founded the company with five friends, and we gave it our all. We now have 140 members and will continue to expand gradually till 2022.

WotNot Team
It's difficult to ignore the impact of technology on business in this day and age, let alone the dizzying speed with which it's growing. Whether you're a large corporation or a small firm, technology advancements like artificial intelligence and cloud databases are rapidly creating an ever-changing blueprint for how we do business in the future.

If we go forward five or fifty years, one thing is sure: technology will revolutionize the corporate landscape as we know it! Even though the term "digital disruption" may feel like a buzzword, the repercussions of its reach and effect have never been more evident.

Since starting WotNot, what have been your main lessons?
It has been a long journey & there have been learnings at each stage of our growth story. Here’s a few off the top of my head:

Invest time in building relationships. Network & learn from other tech entrepreneurs. See what mistakes they are making, & try to prevent them.
Focus on value. Keep track of the industry, but don’t focus too much on competitors. Instead, try to provide as much value to your customers.
Never stop learning. Be a lifelong learner. Regardless of the role you are in, technology is evolving day in & day out & you don’t want to miss out on that.
There will always be problems and fires to put out. You need to assess, pick your battles, and differentiate between good and bad problems. Identify where systems and processes can be tightened to mitigate the same.
Hire people who believe in the vision. Being inspired and learning from each other is what it is all about. Moving ahead in challenging times requires excellent teamwork.


What books & resources do you recommend?
Below I have mentioned some books, which are on my reading list & few podcasts which I am inspired by as a tech entrepreneur:

Books:

The Hard Thing About Hard Things by Ben Horowitz
The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss
The Lean Startup by Eric Ries
The $100 Startup by Chris Guillebeau
Founders at Work by Jessica Livingston
Good to Great: Why Some Companies Make the Leap & Others Don't by Jim Collins
Podcasts:

HBR Idea Cast
This Week in Startups
Masters of Scale
The Tim Ferriss Show
The Future of Everything
‍

Where can we go to learn more?
You can check the Maruti Techlabs website and the Wotnot website. You can also check our socials (LinkedIn, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, Medium, and my personal LinkedIn).

interviews.title: Building India’s Leading Social Commerce Platform
interviews.excerpt: Woovly is a social commerce platform for lifestyle products. Through word of mouth, the company has been growing 30%/month. Here’s how.
interviews.body:
Hi Neha! What's your background, and what are you currently working on?
‍I am Neha Suyal, and I am changing the way small towns and cities of India discover fashion, beauty, and lifestyle products.

Woovly, based in Bangalore, India, is my first entrepreneurial venture. It is India’s leading social commerce platform for fashion, beauty, personal care, and lifestyle products that help customers to shop via AI-driven brand-tagged user-generated content. 

As a qualified Computer Science engineer, I have extensive experience building open-source technologies. I left a well-paying job with HP India in 2015 to join the Stanford Ignite program on Entrepreneurship and Leadership, where I met J. Venkat, my co-founder.

After completing the program, I went on to work with Quess Corp., Venkat’s earlier venture, to understand the business and improve its business metrics.

After working on various Telecom and managed services projects for two years at Quess, I decided to take the plunge as an entrepreneur in 2017 and finally founded Woovly, an adventure experience platform with Venkat in 2019. In 2020, during the pandemic, Woovly pivoted to social commerce for lifestyle products. 

‍

What's your backstory and how did you come up with the idea?
I studied Computer Science Engineering at a Regional Engineering College in Uttarakhand and built my career and expertise at HP, working on open-source technologies. I never had to look far for an idol. 35 years ago, my mother founded the only school in my hometown and continues to run it today. I draw inspiration from my mother’s undying spirit to take on challenges and overcome all odds to fulfill her dreams.

In 2015, I met my co-founder at Stanford, and the idea of Woovly was seeded. We discovered we had a shared interest in studying and predicting consumer buying behavior and our belief that buyers were increasingly tending towards discovering products and brands online rather than offline. 

After the short-term program, I returned to India and worked for two years at Quess Corp. As a part of my responsibilities, I traveled extensively across small towns and cities termed the Tier II and Tier III cities in India and realized that the young population had aspirations to achieve the lifestyle of their peers in Urban India or the Tier I cities. I recognized a latent need for a platform that would allow them to fulfill their ambitions. Later on, when we finally decided to go down the entrepreneurial path, this learning and our faith in online brand discovery led us to social commerce and Woovly.

‍

How did you build Woovly?
During my trips to various Tier II and Tier III towns while working with Quess, I discovered that the youth living there were hard-working and ambitious and wanted to consume lifestyle products too. This made me realize this segment's consumption behavior, which ultimately laid the foundation of Woovly.

I quit Quess in 2017, and Venkat joined me in 2019. We started Woovly as an adventure experience platform but pivoted to social commerce for fashion, beauty, and lifestyle products during the pandemic. 

Our biggest challenge came in early 2020. When the pandemic struck, we had just started getting heavy traction and had over a million users. But travel came to a standstill, and we had to think on our feet to transform ourselves. Our experience with making the perfect blend of content, community, and commerce came in handy and we decided to serve it as a unified experience on our app; this time with fashion, beauty, and lifestyle products.

Which were your marketing strategies to grow your business?
When we started building our business, we were very clear that we did not want to go the social media advertisements route for promotions. We devised our own growth hack since we wanted to grow organically.

For the first 1000 users, we directly reached out, spoke to them, and shared the value proposition. We aimed to make them our ambassadors or brand loyalists who could advocate our brand to their communities. They, in turn, reached out to college students who wanted to be influencers and content creators and brought them on board.

As we began to grow, we also tied up with placements cells of Management Colleges and picked students who wanted to become content creators. Over time, we tied up with 1000 such colleges and 10,000 students. This had a powerful network effect and we were able to make our mark among youngsters organically without spending our resources on costly advertisement campaigns. They became micro and nano influencers with their own groups of followers and we had our community of advocates and loyalists. It was our greatest and most successful marketing strategy.

To date, 72% of our users have been acquired organically i.e., through word of mouth. 61% of our revenue is from these micro and nano influencers.

Woovly Meetup 1
‍

What are your goals for the future?
In the near term, we aim to grow the number of D2C brands featured on our platform by 400% and expand to 4 categories to bring lifestyle products to our users. India is a country of diverse languages, and we aim to reach out to our users in their own language, i.e., vernacular languages.

As per our research, our target audience makes close to Rs. 25000 every month. We hope that by the end of the year, each content creator on the Woovly platform will be able to supplement their income by at least Rs. 12000 per month, on average. This is about 50% of their average monthly income and would help them fulfill their ambition to have a better lifestyle. Our target is to capture 15% of the $100B social commerce market in the next 5 years.

Through the Woovly Creator Academy, we hope to train more young girls across Tier II and Tier III cities so that they can prepare and shoot video content. They can become micro and nano influencers and when they create content and build their community as micro and nano influencers, they get the opportunity to earn a livelihood or supplement their income through incentives on our platform. 

‍

What were the biggest challenges you faced and obstacles you overcame?
Though our business was in a healthy state and we were growing, when Covid hit, we as founders had to take a call on our future. Though it was an unforeseen challenge, we took it positively. Our approach was to work with our core principles and business premise, yet transform to stay relevant and maintain our growth. This move has held us in good stead as we saw 600% growth in our user base in the next 18 months.

The other challenge that I personally, as a women entrepreneur, faced was the unconscious bias around. There are skeptics everywhere - including family, friends, and even peers. Especially because I hail from a small town (Tier III in India), when I quit my job to start my own venture, no one agreed with my decision. It was considered too risky as I was expected to go the conventional route of holding on to a typical day job.

However, with Woovly growing rapidly and setting new benchmarks, I am happy to note that young women find my journey inspirational to start their ventures. 

Woovly Meetup 2
Which are your greatest disadvantages? What were your worst mistakes?
While scaling up, we needed a lot of skilled resources and that’s where I think I fumbled. When the ask was to hire fast, I took a lot of time to hire new talent. When new hires did not perform, I waited too long to let them go, giving them multiple opportunities to come up the curve. In some ways, the slow learners and poor performers slowed down our growth. But very soon, it made me realize that it wasn’t the ideal way to grow. I learned to keep my emotions aside and take tough decisions when necessary.  

Another disadvantage we faced was that we were in unchartered territory. Since social commerce as a concept is still in its early phase in India, we had no benchmarks or standards to measure against. There was nobody to share insights into the industry and we just experimented and built as we progressed. 

‍

If you had the chance to do things differently, what would you do?
Building Woovly has been exciting and enjoyable. I look back at my journey as an immense learning experience. Every obstacle, disadvantage, and challenge have taught me new lessons and I have treated them as learning opportunities. So, there is nothing I would want to do differently. 

‍

What are some sources for learning you would recommend for entrepreneurs who are just starting?
I am an avid reader and love to read on diverse topics related to business, entrepreneurship, and consumer behavior. Predictably Irrational by Dan Ariely is my go-to book for understanding consumer buying behavior.

interviews.title: Ritesh Agarwal’s Entrepreneurial Journey: From Idea to Building OYO
interviews.excerpt: Ritesh Agarwal shares his entrepreneurial journey from identifying challenges in the hospitality industry to building OYO into a technology-driven hospitality company. He discusses his early experiences, the challenges of rapid growth, lessons from entrepreneurship, and his vision for the future of hospitality.
interviews.body:
Who are you and what are you currently working on?

I’m Ritesh Agarwal, the founder and CEO of OYO. My entrepreneurial journey has been focused on building technology-driven solutions for the hospitality industry. Today, OYO works with hotels and accommodation partners to help improve the way travelers discover and book stays.

What inspired you to start OYO?

My interest in entrepreneurship started at a young age. While traveling, I noticed that finding affordable and reliable accommodation could be difficult. There was a clear opportunity to use technology to make the experience easier for both travelers and hotel owners.

What problem were you trying to solve?

The hospitality market had a large number of independent hotels, but many of them lacked technology, branding, and efficient distribution. At the same time, travelers wanted affordable rooms with a more predictable experience. OYO was created to help address both sides of this problem.

How did you go from an idea to building OYO?

The journey started by visiting hotels and understanding the problems faced by owners and customers. Instead of trying to build everything from the beginning, we focused on improving existing properties and creating a more consistent experience for travelers.

What was the biggest challenge when you started?

One of the biggest challenges was convincing hotel owners to change the way they operated. Building trust takes time, especially when you are introducing a new technology-driven model. We had to demonstrate that working with us could create value for their businesses.

Which strategies helped OYO grow?

Technology, partnerships, and a strong focus on customer experience were important parts of our growth. We expanded our network of hotel partners and worked to make booking accommodation simpler for customers.

What did you learn from scaling OYO so quickly?

Rapid growth teaches you that scale brings its own set of challenges. As a company becomes larger, processes, technology, people, and operations all need to evolve. Growth has to be supported by strong fundamentals and the ability to continuously adapt.

What has entrepreneurship taught you?

Entrepreneurship has taught me that there is no perfect roadmap. You have to make decisions with the information available, learn from the results, and keep moving forward. Resilience is extremely important because every entrepreneurial journey comes with uncertainty and setbacks.

If you had to start over, what would you do differently?

I would spend even more time understanding the fundamentals of the business before scaling aggressively. Growth is exciting, but sustainable growth requires strong operations, a clear understanding of customers, and a business model that can support expansion.

What advice would you give to young entrepreneurs?

Don't wait for everything to be perfect before starting. Begin by solving a genuine problem and learn directly from your customers. Be willing to change your approach when the evidence tells you something isn't working. Most importantly, stay persistent.

What is your vision for the future of hospitality?

I believe technology will continue to transform hospitality by making travel more convenient, personalized, and accessible. There is still a huge opportunity to help hotels improve their operations while giving travelers better choices and experiences.

What does success mean to you?

Success is about building something that creates lasting value. Financial performance is important for any business, but I also measure success by the problems we solve, the people we impact, and whether we are able to create something that continues to improve over time.

interviews.title: From a YouTube Teacher to Building Physics Wallah
interviews.excerpt: Alakh Pandey shares his journey from teaching physics on YouTube to building Physics Wallah, his vision of affordable education, the challenges of scaling an EdTech company, and the lessons he learned along the way.
interviews.body:
Who are you and what are you currently working on?

I’m Alakh Pandey, the Founder and CEO of Physics Wallah. My journey has always been closely connected with teaching. What started with teaching physics on YouTube grew into Physics Wallah, with a broader mission of making quality education accessible and affordable for students across India.

Today, PW is focused on building a large education ecosystem that serves students through online, offline, and hybrid learning.

What inspired you to start Physics Wallah?

Teaching was always something I was passionate about. When I started teaching physics, I realized that there were many students who wanted good education but could not afford expensive coaching.

That made me think about how technology could be used to reach a much larger number of students. I started teaching on YouTube in 2014, and the response from students showed me that there was a real need for accessible and affordable educational content.

What problem were you trying to solve?

The biggest problem I wanted to address was access to quality education. A student's ability to learn and achieve their goals should not depend entirely on how much money their family can spend on coaching.

Our approach was to provide quality content and guidance either free or at a minimal cost. The idea was simple: students should be able to access good teachers and learning resources regardless of their economic background.

How did you go from teaching on YouTube to building a company?

Initially, I was focused primarily on teaching. YouTube gave us an opportunity to reach students across different parts of the country without requiring them to physically attend a coaching center.

As the student community grew, we realized that we could build something much larger. In 2020, I joined forces with Prateek Maheshwari, and together we built Physics Wallah into a broader education platform.

What was the biggest challenge when you started scaling Physics Wallah?

Scaling an education platform is very different from simply teaching a class. When you have a growing number of students, you have to think about technology, content, teachers, operations, student support, and maintaining the quality of education.

The challenge was to grow without losing the connection with students and the teaching-focused culture that helped build PW in the first place.

Why did you focus so strongly on affordable education?

I believe education should not become a premium product that is available only to people who can afford it.

There are talented students in every part of the country. Their financial background should not prevent them from getting access to quality learning. That belief has been one of the core principles behind Physics Wallah from the beginning.

Which strategies helped Physics Wallah grow?

One of the biggest strengths was staying close to students and understanding what they actually needed. We started with educational content and gradually expanded the learning experience through technology, study materials, test preparation, apps, and physical learning centers.

We also focused on creating an ecosystem where students could access education through online, offline, and hybrid formats.

How did you deal with competition in the EdTech industry?

Competition is a natural part of any industry. Instead of focusing only on what competitors were doing, our focus was on our students.

If students are getting value from the learning experience, they will continue to trust the platform. For us, the priority has always been teaching quality, accessibility, affordability, and understanding the needs of learners.

What have you learned from your entrepreneurial journey?

I have learned that building a company is very different from having an idea. An idea can start the journey, but execution, patience, teamwork, and the ability to adapt are what help you build something that lasts.

I have also learned that you should never move too far away from the original problem you wanted to solve. For PW, that problem has always been making quality education more accessible.

What role has technology played in your journey?

Technology has allowed us to reach students at a scale that would not have been possible through traditional classrooms alone. A teacher can reach students in different cities and communities through digital platforms.

But technology itself is not the solution. In education, technology needs to support good teaching and learning. That is why we have tried to combine technology with teachers, content, mentorship, and different learning formats. PW's current model includes online, offline, and hybrid education.

If you had to start over, what would you do differently?

I would probably focus on the student problem even more deeply and continue building step by step. When a company grows quickly, there are always many opportunities and distractions.

The important thing is to remember why you started. For us, that means continuing to make education accessible while maintaining the quality and trust that students expect from us.

What advice would you give to young entrepreneurs?

Start with a real problem rather than simply chasing a business trend. If you understand the problem deeply and genuinely care about solving it, you will have a stronger foundation.

Don't be afraid of starting small. Learn from your users, keep improving, and stay patient. Building something meaningful takes time.

What is your vision for the future of education?

My aim is to democratize and transform the education landscape in India. I believe the future of education will combine strong teachers, technology, personalized learning, and multiple ways for students to learn.

Students should be able to access quality education regardless of where they come from or what their financial background is. That is the direction in which I want Physics Wallah to continue growing.

What does success mean to you?

For me, success is not simply about the size of a company. It is about the number of students whose lives we are able to positively impact.

If a student who could not afford expensive coaching gets access to quality education and moves closer to achieving their dream, that is meaningful success. That is what makes the journey worthwhile.

interviews.title: From Identifying a Gap to Building Lenskart
interviews.excerpt: Piyush Bansal shares his entrepreneurial journey, the idea behind Lenskart, the challenges of building a large eyewear business, and the lessons he learned while turning a market gap into a successful startup.
interviews.body:
Who is Piyush Bansal and what is he currently working on?

I’m Piyush Bansal, an entrepreneur and the co-founder and CEO of Lenskart. My journey has been focused on building a technology-driven eyewear business and making eyewear more accessible to consumers.

What inspired you to start Lenskart?

The idea came from seeing a major gap in the eyewear market. Buying glasses was often inconvenient, and consumers had limited choices when it came to discovering and purchasing eyewear. I saw an opportunity to use technology and e-commerce to make the experience simpler and more convenient.

What problem were you trying to solve?

The goal was to make eyewear easier to discover, purchase, and access. We wanted to combine technology, product variety, and an omnichannel experience so customers could have more choices while also getting the convenience of buying through digital platforms.

How did you go from an idea to building the company?

We started by understanding the customer experience and the challenges involved in buying eyewear. Building the business required us to develop technology, create a strong product portfolio, establish operations, and eventually build an offline presence alongside the online platform.

What was one of the biggest challenges when you started?

One of the biggest challenges was changing consumer behaviour. Eyewear is a product that people traditionally prefer to see and try before purchasing. Building confidence in online eyewear purchasing required us to focus heavily on customer experience, technology, product quality, and convenient services.

Which strategies helped Lenskart grow?

Technology and customer experience played an important role. We focused on combining online and offline channels rather than treating them as separate businesses. Expanding our store network, improving technology, offering a wider range of products, and understanding customer needs helped us build the business at scale.

What have you learned from your entrepreneurial journey?

Entrepreneurship has taught me that building a company is a long-term process. You have to continuously understand your customers, experiment with new ideas, and adapt when something doesn't work. Growth is important, but building a sustainable business and creating genuine customer value is equally important.

If you had to start over, what would you do differently?

I would continue focusing on the customer problem first. It is easy for entrepreneurs to become focused on growth, competition, or numbers. But the strongest businesses are built by deeply understanding what customers need and consistently solving that problem better.

What advice would you give to young entrepreneurs?

Start with a real problem and understand it deeply. Don't be afraid of experimentation or failure. Building a company takes patience, resilience, and continuous learning. Most importantly, stay close to your customers and keep improving your product based on what you learn.

What does success mean to you?
